Runtime version stands in for the compiler for JavaScript (same treatment as pure-rand and ultimate-express), and the CPU model is in each record header, so A stands even though the numbers are first-party.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: '1.3~2.5x faster than built-in Intl.Segmenter', '3.5~8x faster than WASM binding of the Rust unicode-segmentation' and '5~48x faster than other JavaScript libraries' in Node.js/Bun/Deno. Record 20260727, Apple M4 Pro, node 26.5.0: ASCII 2.65 us vs Intl.Segmenter 5.30 us (2x), emojis 829.70 ns vs 2.24 us (2.7x), Hindi 2.75 vs 5.44 us (1.98x), demonic characters 457.21 ns vs 1.05 us (2.3x), tweet text 4.12 vs 8.53 us (2.07x), code snippet 9.99 vs 18.97 us (1.9x). Same machine, bun 1.3.14: 1.41x (Hindi) to 2.04x (ASCII) faster than Intl.Segmenter. Record 20251213, Intel Core Ultra 7 258V, node 25.2.1 x64-linux: ASCII 3.71 vs 8.07 us (2.17x), other corpora 2.13x to 3.05x. In Firefox 154.0b1 (20260727, same Mac) it is 1.49x to 1.97x SLOWER than Intl.Segmenter on every corpus.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 112 stars, 4 forks, 324 commits; npm latest 0.17.3 (registry.npmjs.org); listed as an e18e recommendation in the README
corrections.caveats: JavaScript library, not C or C++: outside the default C++ language filter, and it cannot be called from C++ without embedding a JavaScript engine. The baseline is Intl.Segmenter, the JavaScript engine's built-in segmenter: a recognisable incumbent inside JavaScript runtimes, but the timing includes the engine's JS-to-native iterator overhead per segment, so it does not show a win over ICU4C's BreakIterator, HarfBuzz or any C++ library. The other JavaScript libraries (graphemer, grapheme-splitter, @formatjs/intl-segmenter) are weak baselines, and the Rust unicode-segmentation baseline runs as a wasm-bindgen build. Browser results differ: in the 20260727 Firefox 154.0b1 record unicode-segmenter is 1.49x to 1.97x slower than Intl.Segmenter, as the README concedes. The README's Deno claim has no archived record, and its 1.3x lower bound was not found in the three records read (lowest seen: 1.41x in Bun 1.3.14). The 20251213 Node record's file name says nodejs_24.2.1 while its header says node 25.2.1. Numbers are first-party; the harness checks output equality with Intl.Segmenter before timing. Category: this is Unicode text segmentation (wave 3's unicode-utf8 category), not font shaping or layout. The Rust port fast-grapheme-segmenter is a separate entry.

notes: Numbers verified against three record files and perf.js; A kept on the JavaScript precedent (runtime version as compiler). Language corrected from TypeScript to JavaScript (src is .js with JSDoc types); verify.py may ignore the language key, so record a decision override if wanted. Recategorise to Unicode text processing (unicode-utf8), not font-shaping-text-layout.

tier_reason: speedata/typesetting-benchmark's README holds hyperfine output matching every claimed number, from public runners (benchmark.sh, run_typst.sh, run_latex.sh, run_lualatex.sh, mailmerge.typ, mailmerge_template*.tex, mailmerge_*latex.py) on a named machine (MacBook Air M4, 16 GB) with tool versions; it was run by pgundlach of speedata, a competing vendor whose own engine loses at 500 pages, so it is an independent measurement of Typst. Not A: binary builds are unstated, and the timed pipelines are not equivalent (the LaTeX timings include a Python 3.14 + Jinja2 wrapper, fonts differ, and the 500-page input is 500 identical records).

corrections.workload: Mail-merge letters (logo, sender and recipient blocks, justified hyphenated 105 mm body text) built to PDF from XML, 1 page and 500 pages, timed end to end with hyperfine (--warmup 3 for 1 page; --warmup 1 --min-runs 3 for 500 pages). The 500-page input (generate_fakenames.py) is 500 identical copies of one record. Typst reads the XML natively (typst compile --input xml=...); pdflatex and lualatex are driven by a Python script that parses the XML, renders a Jinja2 template and runs one engine pass, and that Python start-up and rendering is inside the timing.
corrections.hardware: MacBook Air M4 (Apple M4), 16 GB RAM, as stated in the README; run by pgundlach (speedata) in February 2026 (3 commits, 2026-02-10 and 2026-02-11).
corrections.caveats: Rust, not C or C++: outside the default C++ language filter. The baselines are document typesetting engines (pdfTeX 1.40.24 and LuaHBTeX 1.15.0 from TeX Live 2022, four years older than Typst 0.14.2), recognisable incumbents for TeX-style typesetting but not HarfBuzz, FreeType or ICU; Typst is a whole typesetting system, so this is a text-layout entry at most. The benchmark comes from speedata (pgundlach, 1-star repo, companion blog post on news.speedata.de that is blocked here; a search snippet says the author would not pick the fastest engine and that a mail merge is the 'hello world' of typesetting). The documents are not equivalent: Typst uses the system 'Helvetica', pdflatex the helvet package (URW Nimbus Sans, Type 1, T1 encoding) and LuaLaTeX TeX Gyre Heros via fontspec; LaTeX sets the sender block in a minipage beside the recipient while Typst places it absolutely; the PDFs are not committed, so page counts could not be checked (each template forces one letter per page). The LaTeX and LuaLaTeX timings include the Python interpreter, Jinja2 import and template rendering; Typst parses the XML itself. The 500-page input is one record repeated 500 times, which favours Typst's memoised layout: 500 pages take 156.6 ms against 105.7 ms for 1 page, about 0.1 ms per extra page (derived from page data), and Typst's user time (241.3 ms) exceeds its wall time, so it used more than one core while pdflatex runs single-threaded. speedata Publisher is fastest at 1 page (94.5 ms, 1.12x faster than Typst). The Typst README claims fast incremental compilation and gives no LaTeX comparison. texlode/luatex-benchmark (MIT, accompanying the TUGboat 2026 paper 'Real-Time LuaTeX: Recompiling Large Documents in 1 ms') reports Typst 0.14 and later about 1.6-2.2x slower per incremental edit than 0.12/0.13 at 300 pages on x86 (no difference on Apple M4), and says the paper's Typst figures came from an earlier script and do not reproduce with bench.mjs (issue #1).

notes: Numbers verified against the speedata README and its runner scripts; B kept as an independent but narrow, non-equivalent shootout. Language Rust is correct (language-filter mismatch). Category: Typst belongs under text layout/typesetting, not font shaping; pdflatex is a typesetting-engine incumbent, not a shaping library.

tier_reason: Every claimed number matches the README tables, which come from the public criterion harness benches/graphemes.rs (criterion 0.8, icu_segmenter 2.3.0 and unicode-segmentation 1.13.3 as dev-dependencies in Cargo.toml), but the page states only 'x86_64 Linux': no CPU model, no rustc version, no flags. First-party with partial methodology is C; the >50x count-mode figure against unicode-segmentation would also be capped at C with flags unstated.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Cargo.toml has no [profile.bench] or [profile.release] override, so cargo's default bench profile applies; edition 2024 implies Rust 1.85 or later; rustc version and target-cpu are not given.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 6 stars, 0 forks, 20 commits; crates.io: 42 total downloads, versions 0.0.0, 0.1.0 and 0.1.1 all published 2026-09-17 (crates.io API, 2026-10-03)
corrections.caveats: Rust crate, not C or C++: outside the default C++ language filter. The baseline is ICU4X's Rust icu_segmenter 2.3.0 (a recognisable Unicode incumbent, but not ICU4C) and the unicode-segmentation crate; this crate's README does not benchmark against Intl.Segmenter, which it only names as the behaviour it replicates. First-party numbers from benches/graphemes.rs (criterion) on 'x86_64 Linux' with no CPU model, rustc version or flags. The samples are about 300 bytes each (UDHR text in eight languages, an emoji string and a Rust snippet), so start-up costs weigh heavily. The headline 35.7x/66.6x is the count-only English path, where printable ASCII is consumed 8 bytes at a time with SWAR masks; in the collect-every-cluster mode the lead over icu_segmenter is 1.3x to 2.0x, and 1.4x to 2.1x when collecting offsets. Forward-only: no backward iteration, seeking or chunked input. The README claims agreement with icu_segmenter on Unicode 17 GraphemeBreakTest.txt and 20,000 pseudo-random strings (tests/conformance.rs, not run here). The repo and crate are about two weeks old (all 20 commits and all three releases on 2026-09-17); it is a port of cometkim/unicode-segmenter by the same author. Category: Unicode text segmentation (wave 3's unicode-utf8 category), not font shaping or layout.

notes: Numbers verified against the README and benches/graphemes.rs; C stands. The orchestrator's note that this compares against Intl.Segmenter does not hold: the bench compares against icu_segmenter (ICU4X) and unicode-segmentation in Rust. Recategorise to Unicode text processing (unicode-utf8); the language key may need a decision override.
